newsitem.title: PERU: Miserable Christmas looms for the hostages in Lima.
newsitem.headline: Miserable Christmas looms for the hostages in Lima.

text.p: More than 140 hostages faced a nightmare Christmas as captives of Marxist gunmen in Peru after the sixth day of the hostage crisis saw no visible progress to end their plight.
Ignoring pleas from President Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul to release the VIP captives, the hostage-takers fell silent on Monday.
There was no public response from the government to the rebels' gesture on Sunday night of freeing 225 hostages. Electricity and water services to the building remained cut.

Unlike previous days, no new signs with messages were thrust up to windows of the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador, and Red Cross officials said no negotiator had entered the building during the day.
Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas stormed the residence last Tuesday during a smart reception to commemorate Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday, taking more than 500 hostages.
Most -- including all the American, British and German captives -- have now been freed.
But the rebels were still holding at gunpoint dozens of top Peruvian governnment officials and about 30 high-ranking Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

The Red Cross was trying to establish the identity of seven of the 225 freed on Sunday night whose names did not match those on a master list of captives to be freed. It was not clear whether the seven had deliberately used false names or whether the confusion was simply an administrative glitch.
Remaining captives in the residence -- and waiting hordes of world media representatives -- could face a long stay.

The rebels, led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, a textile worker turned revolutionary, have demanded that the government set free jailed MRTA comrades before ending the siege, but President Alberto Fujimori has flatly refused.

Fujimori and his interior minister, Gen. Juan Briones Davila, paid a brief first visit on Monday morning to the scene of the siege but did not get out of their bullet-proofed cars or make any comment before driving off, witnesses said.

Adding to the pre-Christmas tension in Lima, police sources told Reuters they believed another clandestine MRTA commando unit was at large in the Peruvian capital and could strike at military targets if the government attacked the rebels in the residence.

Reflecting the grief felt in Japan, Emperor Akihito cancelled all official birthday celebrations on Monday, and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tracked the crisis from a special war room in the Foreign Ministry fitted out with television monitors.

As families of the released hostages celebrated in Lima, Clinton welcomed the freeing of all seven American captives and called for the immediate release of those still held. The pope had earlier added his voice to appeals for an end to the ordeal.

Most Peruvians, long tired of rebel violence, have backed Fujimori's hard line against the rebels. But released hostages said on Monday the lack of water in the residence was endangering the health and safety of those still inside.
"It is extremely important that water is restored," released hostage Victor Lucero told local television. "Water is indispensable. Without it the situation is very dangerous."
Himself a doctor, Lucero said captives had developed at least eight cases of an eye infection because of the unhygeinic conditions. Outbreaks of diarrhoea have also been reported.
The released captives said any attempt to storm the residence would result in heavy loss of life.
The heavily armed, muscular young rebels, numbering around 20, have booby-trapped the entrances of the building and carry backpacks full of explosives.

Police -- who have prepared commandos to storm the residence as a last resort if talks fail -- say the guerrillas include four sharpshooters at strategic windows armed with telescopic night-sight rifles.
About 900 policemen surrounded the residency on Monday, the same number as throughout the crisis.
Salads, chicken and desserts were taken in to feed the captives, and reporters waiting outside behind police lines put up Christmas trees and decorations.

Though police describe MRTA leader Cerpa as a "vicious terrorist" with a long history of bloody attacks, the rebels appear to have treated their captives well and tried to present an image as concerned social crusaders that belies their violent tactics.
